metadata.title: OOPS MCQ Quiz
metadata.description: 100 multiple-choice questions covering the four pillars, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, constructors, keywords, the Object class, nested classes and design principles. Derived one-to-one from the OOPS Learn question bank, so every quiz item reinforces a concept you can go back and read.

questions.question: What is Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)?
options: A style where code is written as a sequence of steps and functions
A programming style that organizes code around objects — real-world entities holding data (fields) and behaviour (methods)
A compiler optimization that converts classes into functions
A database modelling technique for storing records
questions.explanation: OOP models real-world entities as objects that bundle data and behaviour, focusing on reuse, hiding complexity, and maintainability.

questions.question: What are the four main pillars of OOP?
options: Classes, Objects, Methods, Constructors
Association, Aggregation, Composition, Dependency
Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
Overloading, Overriding, Hiding, Shadowing
questions.explanation: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism and Abstraction together make code reusable, secure, flexible and maintainable.

questions.question: What is a class?
options: A blueprint or template describing what an object will look like and what it can do, taking no memory until an object is created
A running instance stored in heap memory
A file that contains only static methods
A reference variable pointing to an object
questions.explanation: A class defines fields (data) and methods (behaviour) but is purely logical — it occupies no runtime memory until you instantiate it.

questions.question: What is an object?
options: A blueprint used to generate classes
A method that returns a value
A package that groups related classes
A real instance of a class created with new, occupying memory with its own state and behaviour
questions.explanation: An object is the physical realization of a class — it has memory, its own field values (state), and access to the class's methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class occupies memory while an object is purely logical
A class is a blueprint (logical, no memory); an object is the actual thing built from it (physical, has memory), and one class can produce many objects
They are the same thing with different names
An object can exist without any class definition
questions.explanation: Class = design, object = product. Many objects can be created from a single class, each with independent state.

questions.question: What are the advantages of OOP?
options: Faster compilation and smaller binaries than procedural code
Direct hardware access and manual memory control
Code reusability via inheritance, easier maintenance, better security via encapsulation, modularity, and clear real-world modelling
Guaranteed absence of runtime errors
questions.explanation: OOP's payoff is structural: reuse, isolation of change, controlled access to data, and a design that mirrors the problem domain.

questions.question: What is the difference between OOP and procedural programming?
options: Procedural programming focuses on functions and sequential steps; OOP groups data and the functions acting on it into objects, which scales better for large systems
OOP is always faster at runtime than procedural code
Procedural programming cannot use variables or loops
OOP forbids the use of functions entirely
questions.explanation: The difference is organizational: procedural code centres on procedures operating on shared data; OOP binds data to the behaviour that owns it.

questions.question: Is Java a purely object-oriented language?
options: Yes, everything in Java is an object
Yes, because it supports all four pillars of OOP
Yes, since primitives are automatically objects
No, because it has primitive types (int, char, boolean) that are not objects
questions.explanation: A purely OO language treats everything as an object. Java's 8 primitives are not objects, so it is not 100% pure.

questions.question: What is a reference variable?
options: A variable that stores a copy of the entire object
A variable that stores the address of an object rather than the object itself
A variable that can only hold primitive values
A variable declared with the final keyword
questions.explanation: In Car c = new Car(); the variable c holds a reference to the Car object living on the heap, not the object itself.

questions.question: Can a class exist without any object being created from it?
options: No, every class must have at least one object to compile
No, the JVM creates a default object automatically
Yes — a class is just a blueprint; it takes no runtime memory until instantiated, and its static members can be used without any object
Yes, but only if the class is declared abstract
questions.explanation: A class exists as a .class file whether or not you instantiate it. Static methods like Math.max() are used without ever creating an object.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
options: Wrapping data and the methods that operate on it into one unit and hiding the internal details, typically via private fields with public getters/setters
Deriving a new class from an existing one
Hiding implementation complexity behind an interface
Allowing one method name to have several parameter lists
questions.explanation: Encapsulation binds state and behaviour into a single class and controls outside access to that state.

questions.question: What are the benefits of encapsulation?
options: It guarantees that the program never throws exceptions
It allows multiple inheritance of classes
It makes all fields globally accessible for convenience
Data security, controlled access with validation inside setters, easier maintenance since internals can change without breaking callers, and cleaner code
questions.explanation: Because callers only touch methods, you can add validation or change the internal representation without breaking any client code.

questions.question: How do you achieve encapsulation in Java?
options: Declare the class as final and all methods as static
Make the fields private and provide public getter and setter methods to read and update them
Mark every field public so subclasses can reach them
Place all related classes into the same package
questions.explanation: Private fields plus public accessors is the standard recipe — the outside world talks to the object only through its methods.

questions.question: What are access modifiers in Java?
options: Keywords that determine how much memory a field consumes
Annotations that control garbage collection of a class
Keywords controlling visibility: private (same class), default (same package), protected (same package plus subclasses), public (everywhere)
Compiler flags passed to javac at build time
questions.explanation: Access modifiers are the mechanism behind data hiding — they define exactly who can see and touch each member.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders private, default, protected and public from most to least restrictive?
options: private → default → protected → public
public → protected → default → private
default → private → public → protected
protected → private → public → default
questions.explanation: private = same class only; default = same package; protected = same package plus child classes even in other packages; public = everywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between data hiding and encapsulation?
options: They are two names for exactly the same thing
Data hiding applies only to static fields; encapsulation only to instance fields
Encapsulation is the goal and data hiding is the tool
Data hiding is the goal — keeping data safe from outside code; encapsulation is the tool that achieves it by bundling data with methods and controlling access
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is the mechanism (bundle + restrict); data hiding is the outcome you want from applying it.

questions.question: How do you create an immutable class in Java?
options: Declare the class abstract and give it only static methods
Declare the class final, make all fields private final, set values only through the constructor, and provide no setters
Mark every field as volatile and synchronize all methods
Override clone() to return the same instance every time
questions.explanation: String is the canonical example. For fields holding mutable objects you must also defensively copy them in the constructor and getters.

questions.question: Can encapsulation exist without data hiding?
options: No, the two are inseparable by definition
No, the compiler rejects a class with public fields
Technically yes — you could bundle data and methods while leaving fields public — but that is bad design, since the protection encapsulation is meant to provide is lost
Yes, and it is the recommended approach for performance
questions.explanation: Bundling alone is not enough. Without private fields there is no control over how state changes, which defeats the purpose.

questions.question: What is inheritance?
options: A mechanism where a child class acquires the fields and methods of a parent class using extends, promoting reuse and an IS-A relationship
A way to hide the internal state of a class from other classes
A technique for creating multiple methods with the same name
A process that copies all the parent's code into the child at compile time
questions.explanation: Inheritance establishes an IS-A relationship and lets a subclass reuse and extend the superclass's behaviour.

questions.question: What are the different types of inheritance?
options: Static, dynamic, virtual and abstract inheritance
Single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple (not supported via classes in Java) and hybrid
Public, private, protected and default inheritance
Direct, indirect, shallow and deep inheritance
questions.explanation: Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical through classes; multiple and hybrid are only achievable through interfaces.

questions.question: Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance with classes?
options: Because the JVM can load only one superclass per program
Because it would make garbage collection impossible
To avoid the Diamond Problem — if a class inherits two parents with the same method, the compiler cannot decide which to use
Because extends and implements are internally identical
questions.explanation: Java sidesteps the ambiguity by allowing a single superclass, while permitting multiple inheritance of type through interfaces.

questions.question: What is the Diamond Problem?
options: An error caused by having too many levels of inheritance
A performance issue when a class has more than four fields
A situation where two classes reference each other in a cycle
Ambiguity when a class inherits from two parents sharing the same method, so the compiler cannot decide which version to use
questions.explanation: Java prevents it for classes outright; for interfaces with conflicting default methods it forces the implementing class to resolve the conflict explicitly.

questions.question: What does the extends keyword do?
options: It inherits from a class — the child gets all non-private members of the parent and may add its own or override existing ones
It implements an interface contract in a class
It merges two classes into one at compile time
It prevents a class from being subclassed further
questions.explanation: class Dog extends Animal creates the IS-A relationship. Classes use extends for classes and implements for interfaces.

questions.question: What does the super keyword do?
options: It refers to the topmost Object class in every hierarchy
It references the immediate parent class — super.method() calls a parent method, super.field accesses a parent field, and super(...) invokes the parent constructor
It gives a subclass access to the parent's private members
It marks a method as non-overridable
questions.explanation: super is how a child reaches its immediate parent, most commonly to chain constructors or to extend rather than fully replace an overridden method.

questions.question: What is an IS-A relationship?
options: A relationship created by declaring a field of another class type
A relationship that only exists between interfaces
The relationship inheritance creates — if class X extends class Y then X IS-A Y and can be used anywhere Y is expected
A relationship where two classes have identical method signatures
questions.explanation: IS-A is what makes polymorphic substitution legal: an Animal reference can hold a Dog because Dog IS-A Animal.

questions.question: What is a HAS-A relationship?
options: A relationship created using the extends keyword
A relationship where two classes implement the same interface
A relationship between a class and its static members
A relationship where one class holds a reference to another (composition/aggregation) — for example class Car { Engine e; } means Car HAS-A Engine
questions.explanation: HAS-A models containment rather than type identity, and is usually the more flexible choice.

questions.question: What is the difference between inheritance and composition?
options: Inheritance is IS-A and creates tight coupling; composition is HAS-A and is more flexible — the modern guidance is to favour composition unless there is a genuine IS-A relationship
Composition is IS-A and inheritance is HAS-A
Composition can only be used with abstract classes
Inheritance is always preferred because it produces less code
questions.explanation: Inheritance locks the child to the parent's implementation. Composition lets you swap the contained object and change behaviour at runtime.

questions.question: Can a subclass access private members of its parent class?
options: Yes, private members are always visible to subclasses
No — private members are class-scoped, so the subclass can only reach them indirectly through the parent's public or protected methods
Yes, but only if both classes are in the same package
No, and the private fields are not even allocated in the child object
questions.explanation: The private fields do exist inside the subclass instance as part of the parent's layout, but the compiler denies direct access — that is what protected is for.

questions.question: Are constructors inherited in Java?
options: Yes, exactly like public methods
Yes, but only no-argument constructors are inherited
No — constructors are not inherited; each class has its own, and the child constructor implicitly calls the parent's via super() to initialize inherited fields
No, and the parent constructor never runs when a child is created
questions.explanation: Constructors are not members that get inherited, but the parent constructor always executes first in the chain when a child object is built.

questions.question: What happens if a child constructor doesn't explicitly call super()?
options: The parent constructor is skipped entirely
The code fails to compile in all cases
The child constructor runs before the parent constructor
Java automatically inserts a no-arg super() as the first line — and if the parent has no no-arg constructor, the code will not compile unless you call super(...) explicitly
questions.explanation: This is why adding a parameterized constructor to a parent can suddenly break every subclass — the implicit no-arg super() no longer resolves.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: 'One name, many forms' — the same method name or reference behaves differently depending on context
The ability to hide fields behind getters and setters
The ability of a class to inherit from several parents
The process of converting an object into a byte stream
questions.explanation: Polymorphism appears in two forms in Java: compile-time via overloading and runtime via overriding.

questions.question: What are the types of polymorphism in Java?
options: Public and private polymorphism
Compile-time (static) polymorphism via method overloading, and runtime (dynamic) polymorphism via method overriding
Shallow and deep polymorphism
Single and multiple polymorphism
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved by the compiler from the argument list; overriding is resolved by the JVM from the actual object type.

questions.question: What is method overloading?
options: A subclass replacing a parent method with its own version
Declaring the same method twice with identical signatures
Defining several methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists (different count, types or order)
Calling a method before the object is constructed
questions.explanation: The compiler chooses the matching overload from the arguments you pass. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

questions.question: What is method overriding?
options: Declaring two methods with the same name in one class
Hiding a parent's static method behind a subclass version
Preventing a method from being called by subclasses
When a subclass provides its own implementation of a method already defined in the parent, using the same signature, resolved at runtime by the actual object type
questions.explanation: Overriding is the basis of runtime polymorphism — the JVM dispatches to the child's version even through a parent-typed reference.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading: same class, different parameters, compile-time, no inheritance needed. Overriding: parent-child classes, same signature, runtime, requires inheritance
Overloading requires inheritance while overriding does not
Overloading is resolved at runtime and overriding at compile time
Both require identical parameter lists and different return types
questions.explanation: Overloading is 'same name, different work'; overriding is 'same work, different class'.

questions.question: What is the difference between static binding and dynamic binding?
options: Static binding happens for overridden methods and dynamic binding for overloaded ones

Static (early) binding resolves the call at compile time — used for overloaded, private, static and final methods; dynamic (late) binding resolves it at runtime from the actual object — used for overridden methods
Both resolve at runtime and differ only in speed
Dynamic binding applies only to static methods
questions.explanation: Anything the compiler can decide with certainty is bound early; anything depending on the real object type is deferred to runtime.

questions.question: Can you override a static method in Java?
options: Yes, exactly like an instance method
Yes, provided the subclass is in the same package
No — static methods belong to the class, so redefining one in a subclass is method hiding rather than overriding, and polymorphism does not apply
No, and the compiler rejects any static method with the same name in a subclass
questions.explanation: With method hiding the call is resolved from the reference type at compile time, not from the object at runtime.

questions.question: Can you overload the main() method?
options: No, main() is special and cannot be overloaded
No, the compiler reports a duplicate method error
Yes, but the program will then fail to start
Yes — you can define several main methods with different parameters, but the JVM always calls public static void main(String[] args) to start the program
questions.explanation: Overloaded mains are ordinary methods; only the exact String[] signature serves as the entry point, and the others must be called explicitly.

questions.question: Can you override a private method?
options: No — private methods are not visible to subclasses, so a same-signature method in the child is simply a brand-new method, not an override
Yes, provided you add the @Override annotation
Yes, private methods are overridden implicitly
No, and defining a same-named method in the child is a compile-time error
questions.explanation: Because private methods are invisible to the subclass they are bound statically. Adding @Override to such a method is a compile error, which is a good way to catch the mistake.

questions.question: Can you override a final method?
options: Yes, if the subclass method is also declared final
No — final on a method means it cannot be overridden by any subclass, and attempting to do so is a compile-time error
Yes, but only within the same package
Yes, final only prevents the variable from being reassigned
questions.explanation: final on a method locks its behaviour for the whole hierarchy — often used to protect logic that subclasses must not change.

questions.question: What is a covariant return type?
options: A return type that changes depending on the arguments passed
A return type that must be identical in parent and child
When an overriding method returns a subclass of what the parent method returned — for example the parent returns Animal and the child returns Dog (allowed since Java 5)
A return type declared with the var keyword
questions.explanation: Covariant returns let an override be more specific, so callers avoid a downcast. Before Java 5 the return type had to match exactly.

questions.question: What is method hiding?
options: Making a method private so subclasses cannot see it
Using the final keyword to lock a method's implementation
Declaring a method inside a nested class to limit its scope
When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method — it hides rather than overrides, and the call is resolved at compile time from the reference type
questions.explanation: This is why calling a hidden static method through a parent-typed reference runs the parent's version, which surprises people expecting polymorphism.

questions.question: Can overloaded methods have different return types?
options: Yes they can — but the return type alone is not enough to overload; the parameter lists must also differ, otherwise the compiler reports an ambiguity error
No, all overloads must return exactly the same type
Yes, and differing return types alone are sufficient to overload
Only if the return types are related by inheritance
questions.explanation: Overload resolution uses the argument list only, so two methods differing solely in return type cannot be distinguished.

questions.question: Which set of rules applies to method overriding in Java?
options: The override may narrow the access modifier and throw broader checked exceptions

Same name, same parameters, same or covariant return type; access cannot be more restrictive than the parent; static, final and private methods cannot be overridden; and the override may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions
The parameter list may differ as long as the name matches
The override must always be declared final
questions.explanation: Widening access is allowed (protected → public) but narrowing is not, since that would break substitutability.

questions.question: What is abstraction?
options: Bundling fields and methods into a single class
Creating multiple objects from a single class
Hiding internal complexity and exposing only what matters — using a feature without knowing how it is built; achieved in Java through abstract classes and interfaces
Copying an object's state into a new independent object
questions.explanation: Abstraction is about the WHAT rather than the HOW — you press the brake pedal without knowing the hydraulics behind it.

questions.question: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation?
options: They are two words for the same concept
Abstraction hides data while encapsulation hides complexity
Abstraction applies only to interfaces and encapsulation only to classes

Abstraction hides complexity by showing only WHAT, not HOW; encapsulation hides data by bundling fields with methods and restricting access. Abstraction is a design concern, encapsulation an implementation one
questions.explanation: You abstract at the design level (what the type promises) and encapsulate at the implementation level (how the state is protected).

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
options: A class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated and may hold both abstract methods (no body) and concrete methods (with body)
A class containing only static methods and constants
A class that has no fields at all
A class that can be instantiated but not subclassed
questions.explanation: Abstract classes sit between a full implementation and a pure contract — they share code while forcing subclasses to fill in the gaps.

questions.question: What is an abstract method?
options: A method whose body is generated automatically by the compiler
A method declared with abstract and no body — just a signature followed by a semicolon — which can exist only inside an abstract class or an interface
A method that can only be called from within the same package
A method that returns no value
questions.explanation: Any concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method, or be declared abstract itself.

questions.question: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
options: No, because abstract classes cannot be instantiated
No, the compiler removes it automatically
Yes — even though you cannot instantiate it directly, its constructor runs when a subclass object is created, initializing the abstract class's fields via super()
Yes, but only a no-argument constructor is permitted
questions.explanation: Every object construction walks the whole chain, so an abstract parent still needs a constructor to set up its own state.

questions.question: Can you instantiate an abstract class?
options: Yes, using the new keyword like any other class
Yes, if all of its methods happen to be concrete
Yes, but only from inside the same package
No — abstract classes are incomplete by design; you can only create objects of their concrete subclasses, and new AbstractClass() is a compile-time error
questions.explanation: You can, however, write new AbstractClass() { ... } — that is an anonymous subclass, not an instance of the abstract class itself.

questions.question: Can an abstract class have concrete (non-abstract) methods?
options: Yes — that is one of its main advantages: it can define shared behaviour in concrete methods while forcing subclasses to implement the abstract ones
No, every method in an abstract class must be abstract
Yes, but only static methods may have bodies
No, concrete methods are allowed only in interfaces
questions.explanation: This mix is exactly what distinguishes an abstract class from a pre-Java-8 interface — shared implementation plus mandatory contract.

questions.question: Can an abstract class be declared final?
options: Yes, to prevent further subclassing beyond the first level
No — abstract means 'must be subclassed' and final means 'cannot be subclassed', so the two contradict and the compiler reports an error
Yes, but only if it contains no abstract methods
Yes, and it is a common way to create utility classes
questions.explanation: A final abstract class could never be used, since it can neither be instantiated nor extended.

questions.question: What is an interface in Java?
options: A class that cannot have any methods
A special class used only for exception handling
A 100% abstract type (pre-Java 8) defining a contract of methods a class must implement — since Java 8 it can also have default and static methods, and since Java 9 private methods
A container that holds objects of different types
questions.explanation: Interfaces express capability (CAN-DO) and are the mechanism through which Java supports multiple inheritance of type.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
options: An interface can have constructors and instance fields while an abstract class cannot
An abstract class supports multiple inheritance while an interface supports only single
They became functionally identical in Java 8

Abstract class: fields, constructors, concrete and abstract methods, single inheritance. Interface: primarily abstract methods plus default/static since Java 8, no constructors, multiple inheritance allowed
questions.explanation: Use an abstract class for an IS-A relationship with shared code and state; use an interface for a CAN-DO contract, especially when multiple inheritance is needed.

questions.question: Can an interface extend another interface?
options: Yes — an interface can extend one or several other interfaces using extends (not implements), inheriting all their abstract methods
No, only classes can use extends
Yes, but only a single parent interface is allowed
No, interfaces must use implements to inherit from one another
questions.explanation: Interface-to-interface inheritance uses extends and permits multiple parents, which is how Java gets multiple inheritance of type.

questions.question: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
options: No, a class may implement at most one interface
Yes — Java supports multiple interface inheritance, so a class can implement any number, as in class Car implements Drivable, Fuelable, Serializable
Yes, but only if the interfaces have no methods in common
No, unless the class is declared abstract
questions.explanation: Because interfaces carry no state, combining several creates no diamond ambiguity — only conflicting default methods need explicit resolution.

questions.question: What are default methods in interfaces?
options: Methods invoked automatically when no other method matches
Methods generated by the compiler for every interface
Methods with a body inside an interface, marked with the default keyword (Java 8+), which allow new methods to be added without breaking existing implementing classes
Private helper methods usable only inside the interface
questions.explanation: Default methods solved interface evolution — they are how forEach() could be added to Collection without breaking every existing implementation.

questions.question: Can an interface have a constructor?
options: Yes, but it must be declared private
Yes, and it runs when an implementing class is instantiated
Yes, since Java 8 introduced default constructors for interfaces
No — interfaces cannot be instantiated so they need no constructors, and their fields are implicitly public static final, assigned at declaration
questions.explanation: There is no interface state to initialize: every field is a compile-time constant set where it is declared.

questions.question: Can an interface have variables?
options: Yes, but every variable is implicitly public static final — a constant — so instance variables are not allowed
No, interfaces cannot declare any variables
Yes, and they behave exactly like ordinary instance fields
Yes, but only private variables are permitted
questions.explanation: interface Config { int MAX = 100; } declares a constant. You cannot give an interface mutable per-object state.

questions.question: What is a marker interface?
options: An interface containing exactly one abstract method
An interface with no methods or fields, used to 'mark' a class for special treatment by the JVM or a framework — Serializable and Cloneable are examples
An interface that can only be implemented by abstract classes
An interface annotated with @Marker
questions.explanation: The marker carries no behaviour; code checks for it with instanceof and changes its handling accordingly. Annotations have largely replaced this pattern.

questions.question: When should you choose an abstract class over an interface?
options: Always prefer an abstract class, since interfaces are legacy
Choose an interface whenever the classes share common code
Use an abstract class when classes share common code and state (an IS-A relationship); use an interface when you only need to specify a behavioural contract (CAN-DO) or need multiple inheritance
Choose based on which one has fewer methods
questions.explanation: Abstract classes give you shared implementation and fields; interfaces give you flexible, multiply-inheritable contracts.

questions.question: What is a constructor?
options: A method that runs just before an object is garbage collected
A static method that returns a new instance of the class
A block that executes once when the class is first loaded
A special block sharing the class's name that runs automatically on object creation to initialize fields, and which has no return type — not even void
questions.explanation: The absence of a return type is what syntactically distinguishes a constructor from a method with the same name as the class.

questions.question: What are the types of constructors in Java?
options: Default (no args, compiler-generated if none is defined), parameterized (accepts arguments), and copy (takes another object of the same class, which you must write yourself)
Public, private, protected and default constructors
Static, final and abstract constructors
Primary, secondary and virtual constructors
questions.explanation: Unlike C++, Java never generates a copy constructor for you — you have to write it.

questions.question: What is the difference between a constructor and a method?
options: A constructor can have any name while a method must match the class name

A constructor shares the class name, has no return type and runs automatically on object creation to initialize state; a method has any name, has a return type, and is called explicitly to define behaviour
Both run automatically when an object is created
A method cannot be overloaded but a constructor can
questions.explanation: Constructors initialize; methods operate. A constructor is invoked exactly once per object, by new.

questions.question: Can a constructor be declared final?
options: Yes, to prevent subclasses from redefining it
Yes, and it is required for immutable classes
No — constructors are not inherited, so preventing overriding is meaningless, and the compiler reports an error
Yes, but only in a final class
questions.explanation: final exists to block overriding. Since constructors are never inherited or overridden, the modifier has nothing to do.

questions.question: Can a constructor be declared static?
options: Yes, for singleton classes
Yes, static constructors run before any instance is created
Yes, but only one per class
No — constructors operate on instances while static means 'belongs to the class, not any instance', so the two contradict and it is not allowed
questions.explanation: A static initializer block ({ static { ... } }) is the class-level counterpart, but it is not a constructor.

questions.question: Can a constructor be declared abstract?
options: No — abstract means no body, but a constructor must have a body to initialize the object, so the compiler rejects it
Yes, inside an abstract class
Yes, and subclasses must then implement it
Yes, provided the class has no fields
questions.explanation: Even abstract classes have ordinary, concrete constructors that run during subclass instantiation.

questions.question: What is constructor overloading?
options: Calling one constructor from inside another
Defining several constructors in the same class with different parameter lists, so objects can be created in multiple ways such as new Car(), new Car("Tesla") and new Car("Tesla", 2025)
Providing a constructor in both the parent and the child class
Declaring a constructor that accepts a variable number of arguments
questions.explanation: Constructor overloading follows exactly the same rules as method overloading — the parameter lists must differ.

questions.question: What is constructor chaining?
options: Creating several objects in a single statement
Declaring constructors in a parent-child hierarchy
Calling one constructor from another — this(...) within the same class, or super(...) to reach the parent — which must be the very first statement of the constructor
Automatically generating constructors for all subclasses
questions.explanation: Chaining avoids duplicated initialization logic. Because this(...) and super(...) must both come first, you can use only one of them per constructor.

questions.question: What is a copy constructor, and does Java provide one automatically?
options: It duplicates an object and Java generates it automatically for every class
It is produced automatically whenever you call clone()
It is a synonym for the default constructor
It creates a new object by copying the fields of another object of the same class — and Java does NOT provide one automatically, unlike C++, so you write it yourself
questions.explanation: You must also decide whether to copy nested objects (deep) or share their references (shallow).

questions.question: What happens if you don't define any constructor in a class?
options: The compiler inserts a default no-arg constructor that calls super() and leaves fields at their default values — but as soon as you define any constructor, that default is no longer added
The class cannot be instantiated at all
The JVM throws a NoConstructorException at runtime
Fields are left uninitialized and reading them causes a compile error
questions.explanation: This is why adding a single parameterized constructor can break existing new MyClass() calls — the implicit no-arg constructor disappears.

questions.question: Can you call a constructor from an ordinary method?
options: Yes, this() and super() can be called from any method
Not directly — this(...) and super(...) are only legal inside a constructor — but a method can create a new object with new ClassName(...), which does invoke a constructor
Yes, but only from a static method
No, and a method cannot create objects either
questions.explanation: The restriction exists because this() and super() are part of the object-initialization sequence, which happens once, at construction.

questions.question: What does the static keyword do?
options: It makes a variable's value permanently unchangeable
It prevents a class from being subclassed
It marks a field, method, block or nested class as belonging to the class itself rather than to any instance — shared across all objects and loaded once when the class loads
It forces an object to stay in memory for the program's lifetime
questions.explanation: Static members exist exactly once per class, regardless of how many objects you create — or whether you create any at all.

questions.question: What is the difference between a static method and an instance method?
options: A static method can access instance fields directly while an instance method cannot
Instance methods are shared across all objects while static methods are per-object
There is no functional difference, only a naming convention

A static method belongs to the class, is called as ClassName.method(), has no this reference and cannot touch instance members directly; an instance method belongs to an object and has full access to this and its fields
questions.explanation: The absence of this is the root cause — a static method has no object to resolve instance members against.

questions.question: What is a static block?
options: A block marked static { ... } that runs once when the class is first loaded, before any object is created — typically used to initialize static fields
A block that runs before every method call
A synchronized block that only one thread may enter
A block that runs each time an object is constructed
questions.explanation: Static blocks run in declaration order at class-load time. The per-object counterpart is the instance initializer block, written without static.

questions.question: Can a static method access non-static members directly?
options: Yes, static methods have full access to all class members
No — a static method runs without an instance, so it cannot touch instance fields or call instance methods directly; you must create an object first and go through it
Yes, but only if the members are declared protected
No, and it cannot access static members either
questions.explanation: This is exactly why main() cannot call an instance method without first creating an object — it is static and has no this.

questions.question: What does the final keyword do?
options: It makes a member belong to the class rather than to instances
It marks a method as automatically synchronized
It restricts modification: a final variable is a constant that cannot be reassigned, a final method cannot be overridden, and a final class cannot be subclassed
It causes an object to be garbage collected immediately
questions.explanation: String is the best-known final class — making it non-extendable is part of what guarantees its immutability.

questions.question: What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize()?
options: All three are exception-handling constructs
final closes resources, finally makes variables constant, finalize() triggers the garbage collector
final and finalize() are identical while finally is a loop

final is a keyword for constants / non-overridable methods / non-extendable classes; finally is a block that always runs after try/catch for cleanup; finalize() was a GC callback, deprecated since Java 9
questions.explanation: Three unrelated concepts that share a prefix — a favourite trick question.

questions.question: What does the this keyword refer to?
options: A reference to the current object — used to access instance fields, call another constructor via this(...), or pass the current object to a method
A reference to the parent class object
A reference to the class definition itself
A keyword valid only inside static methods
questions.explanation: this is most commonly used to disambiguate a constructor parameter from the field it initializes: this.name = name;

questions.question: What is the difference between this and super?
options: this refers to the parent class and super to the current object

this is the current object reference (this class's members, and this class's other constructors via this()); super is the parent class reference (parent's members, and the parent constructor via super())
Both refer to the same object and differ only in syntax
super can only be used inside static methods
questions.explanation: Since both this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement of a constructor, only one of them can appear in any given constructor.

questions.question: Can a final variable be reassigned?
options: Yes, once per method invocation
Yes, provided it is also declared static
No — once assigned it cannot be changed; for a final reference the reference itself is locked, though the referenced object's internal state can still be mutated unless that object is immutable
No, and the referenced object can never be modified either
questions.explanation: final List<String> l = new ArrayList<>(); forbids l = somethingElse but still permits l.add("x") — a very common exam trap.

questions.question: What is the Object class in Java?
options: An interface every class must implement explicitly
A utility class holding static helper methods
An abstract class that cannot be extended
The root of the Java class hierarchy — every class inherits from java.lang.Object directly or indirectly, gaining equals(), hashCode(), toString(), clone(), getClass(), wait() and notify()
questions.explanation: This is why any object can be assigned to an Object reference and why every object already has a toString().

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals()?
options: == compares references (whether they point to the same object in memory) while .equals() compares content as defined by the class
.equals() compares references and == compares content
Both compare content identically for every class
== works only on primitives and .equals() only on Strings
questions.explanation: Object.equals() defaults to == behaviour, so you must override it for value-based classes such as your own domain objects.

questions.question: What is the contract between hashCode() and equals()?
options: Objects with equal hash codes must always be equal
If a.equals(b) is true then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode() — but equal hash codes do NOT imply the objects are equal
hashCode() must return a unique value for every object
The two methods are independent and need not agree
questions.explanation: The one-way implication is the key point: equality forces equal hashes, but a hash collision says nothing about equality.

questions.question: Why must you override hashCode() whenever you override equals()?
options: Because the compiler refuses to build otherwise
Because equals() calls hashCode() internally
Because hash-based collections use hashCode() to pick the bucket — if two 'equal' objects return different hash codes they land in different buckets and lookups fail
Because hashCode() is abstract in Object and must be implemented
questions.explanation: The classic symptom: you put an object into a HashSet, then contains() on an equal object returns false.

questions.question: What does the toString() method do?
options: It converts a String into an object
It compares two objects and returns a String verdict
It serializes the object to disk
It returns a String representation of the object; the default Object.toString() returns ClassName@hashcode, so you override it to print meaningful information for logging and debugging
questions.explanation: toString() is called implicitly during string concatenation and by println(), which is why an unoverridden object prints as com.example.User@1b6d3586.

questions.question: What does clone() do, and what is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
options: clone() creates a copy of an object. A shallow copy duplicates fields as-is so nested object references are shared; a deep copy recursively duplicates nested objects, producing a fully independent duplicate
clone() always produces a deep copy automatically
A shallow copy duplicates nested objects while a deep copy shares them
clone() returns the same object reference, so no copy is made
questions.explanation: Object.clone() is shallow by default — mutating a nested object through either reference is visible from both.

questions.question: What is the finalize() method?
options: A method that runs immediately after a constructor completes

A method the garbage collector called before reclaiming an object, allowing last-minute cleanup — deprecated since Java 9 because it is unreliable and slow, with try-with-resources or Cleaner as the replacement
A method that forces an object to be collected right away
A method that makes an object immutable
questions.explanation: There was never any guarantee finalize() would run at all, or when, which is why resource cleanup moved to AutoCloseable and try-with-resources.

questions.question: What is a nested class?
options: A class that extends more than one parent
A class declared inside a method only
A class defined inside another class — the four kinds being static nested, (non-static) inner, local (inside a method) and anonymous (unnamed, defined inline)
A class stored in a subdirectory of its package
questions.explanation: Nesting is used to group a helper type tightly with the class that uses it, keeping it out of the package namespace.

questions.question: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class?
options: An inner class can be instantiated without any outer object while a static nested class cannot
Both require an instance of the outer class
Static nested classes cannot access any members of the outer class, not even static ones

A static nested class behaves like a top-level class and needs no outer instance; a non-static inner class is tied to an outer instance, can access the outer object's fields directly, and requires an outer object to create
questions.explanation: Because an inner class holds an implicit reference to its outer instance, it can also prevent that outer object from being garbage collected.

questions.question: What is an anonymous inner class?
options: A nameless class declared and instantiated in a single expression, typically to override a method or implement an interface inline — largely replaced by lambdas since Java 8 for functional interfaces
A class whose name is generated randomly by the compiler
A class with no methods or fields
A class that cannot be referenced from anywhere in the program
questions.explanation: new Runnable() { public void run() { ... } } is the classic form; for a functional interface a lambda now expresses the same thing far more briefly.

questions.question: What is a local inner class?
options: A class defined inside a package but not exported
A class defined inside a method or block, scoped to that method, which can access the enclosing method's local variables only if they are final or effectively final
A class that can only be used by classes in the same file
A nested class marked with the local keyword
questions.explanation: The final/effectively-final restriction exists because the local variable's value is captured by copy — the class may outlive the method call.

questions.question: What is the difference between association, aggregation and composition?
options: All three describe the same IS-A relationship
Aggregation is stronger than composition

Association is a general HAS-A relationship; aggregation is a weak HAS-A where the parts can exist independently (a Department has Professors); composition is a strong HAS-A where the parts cannot exist without the whole (a House has Rooms)
Composition is created with extends and aggregation with implements
questions.explanation: The test is lifecycle ownership: destroy the House and its Rooms go with it; close the Department and the Professors still exist.

questions.question: What are coupling and cohesion?
options: Coupling should be high and cohesion low for best design
They are two names for the same design metric
Coupling measures how many methods a class has; cohesion measures how many fields

Coupling is how much one class depends on another (lower is better); cohesion is how focused a class is on a single responsibility (higher is better). Good OOP design means loose coupling and high cohesion
questions.explanation: Loose coupling makes change safe; high cohesion makes a class easy to understand and reuse.

questions.question: What do the SOLID principles stand for?
options: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion
Simple, Organized, Logical, Independent, Documented
Static, Object-oriented, Layered, Isolated, Decoupled
Structured, Optimized, Linked, Inherited, Delegated
questions.explanation: Five design principles that together push a codebase toward small, focused, substitutable and loosely coupled types.

questions.question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
options: A class should expose only one public method
A class should have only one reason to change — it should do one thing well, and be split up if it takes on too many responsibilities
A method should accept only one parameter
A package should contain only one class
questions.explanation: 'One reason to change' is about who requests the change: if reporting and persistence changes both hit the same class, it has two responsibilities.

questions.question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
options: A subclass must override every method of its parent
A class should be open for extension but closed for modification
Subclasses must be usable in place of their parent class without breaking the program — anywhere an Animal is expected, a Dog should work without surprising behaviour
Classes should depend on concrete implementations rather than abstractions
questions.explanation: The classic violation is Square extends Rectangle: setting width and height independently breaks the behaviour callers rely on.

questions.question: What is dependency injection?
options: A technique for injecting code into a running JVM
A way for a class to create all of its own dependencies internally
A method for merging two classes at compile time
A pattern where a class receives the objects it depends on from outside — via constructor, setter or field — instead of creating them itself, reducing coupling and simplifying testing
questions.explanation: Because the dependency is supplied, tests can pass a mock or stub. Frameworks like Spring automate the wiring.

questions.question: Which of these are common OOP design patterns?
options: Singleton (one instance), Factory (create without exposing the class), Builder (step-by-step construction), Observer (publish-subscribe), Strategy (pluggable algorithm), Decorator (wrap to add behaviour), Adapter (bridge incompatible interfaces)
Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism and Abstraction
Compile-time, runtime, static and dynamic patterns
Public, private, protected and default patterns
questions.explanation: Patterns are reusable solutions to recurring design problems, grouped as creational, structural and behavioural.

questions.question: What is the Singleton pattern?
options: A pattern that creates a new instance for every request
A pattern ensuring a class has only one instance and providing a global access point to it — implemented with a private constructor and a static getInstance() method
A pattern where one class inherits from exactly one parent
A pattern that stores a single field per object
questions.explanation: The private constructor blocks external instantiation. In multithreaded code the instance must be created safely — via an enum, a static holder class, or double-checked locking with volatile.
